name: Erik Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. How did your workday begin?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik Moreau, fifty-eight, a junior accountant at West Arch Accounts, mostly on small concert venues' accounts and tax returns. I like finding why a refund belongs to a different show; the late crumpled till rolls make me wish the box office had a better drawer. My partner Elise works at a library, and our grown children have their own households.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get onto the accounts desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I came into accounting later and earned a bachelor's degree in accounting, so I still ask the senior about unusual tax deposits. I use a tested AI note tool now and then for missing-receipt lists, but I reconcile the figures myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ticket-hall clients at West Arch Accounts that a modest sorter is welcome as long as somebody still checks the cash sheet after a show. The queue at the door is real even if the totals arrive by email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am junior and still slower than the senior at tax adjustments, but the venue work pays me well for this level. My partner and I have about ten months of expenses saved and plenty of accounting firms nearby, so a small gain does not threaten today's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching ticket refunds to the night manager's cash sheet and ask the senior to check the tax treatment of unusual deposits. I'd move seventy from each month's pay into our home-repair account while we both have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this ordinary season. Retirement is in sight, but I would still check the actual household figures before promising a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a good day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I found a refund recorded against the wrong concert and the box-office manager stopped arguing with the promoter. I like that click when two people can use the same sheet; the late crumpled till rolls are the tiresome part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use an approved tool to draft a list of missing receipts after a colleague tests it. I still reconcile the figures myself because I am learning. A neat AI receipt list can hide the wrong concert night.

I'd have a **senior reviewer** sign unusual tax treatments on concert deposits.
think: My **higher junior pay** seems safe under a minor sorter.
Ten months saved and **many local firms** give us room.
do: Match **ticket refunds** to the night manager's original cash sheet.
Save **seventy monthly** from wages for home repairs while both jobs hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about my current pay.

steps.text: Keep matching ticket refunds to venue cash sheets with senior tax review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask West Arch to show the box-office managers the new system's missed refunds before promising a cheaper return. A fast report cannot give a promoter the cash that vanished from the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tool that writes client replies and reconciles receipts could take the junior part of my job, even though I have learned to use a few approved notes. We can search with our ten-month cushion, but I don't want to spend it replacing a wage the firm still owes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for two paid sessions on closed concert files to learn the new refund-matching screen, with the senior checking missed refunds and repair time before any live use. In the first year of steady change, if West Arch removes a paid day, I'd apply to posted junior accounting openings at nearby firms and keep offered West Arch hours until written pay covering our bills and an actual start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own paid week shrinking. A tested screen is fine; a shortened rota is a different matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners deny paid sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our approved refund ledger and ask for a written hours plan. I wouldn't send live ticket sales through a new tool at home to prove I can learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a good trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the missed refunds with the old cash sheets and time each correction. If the figures hold over both paid sessions, I'd use the screen; if not, I'd show the partner the errors before signing.

I'd ask for **paid practice time** on old concert files before live use.
think: My **junior paid day** could disappear when software takes over refund and reply work.
The cushion buys search time but cannot replace **permanent wages** from this desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell venue owners full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking in accounts and tax returns before robots reach the physical ticket gate around 2031. My tax desk cannot borrow the three years before ticket-gate robots arrive. I'd ask the concert hall for a real posted paid payroll vacancy before calling it my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect West Arch to cut most routine review posts, including mine. My partner Elise's library wage and ten months saved would keep us steady for a while, but my higher junior pay is part of our regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the current seventy-five monthly concert package and add that amount from wages to cash now. In the first year after 2028, if West Arch ends my post, I'd apply for advertised paid payroll work at the local concert hall, keeping any paid West Arch closeout returns only while offered until written bill-covering pay and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect my own wage to stop quickly. The hall itself might need payroll staff, but AGI reaches that office too, so I cannot call the building a refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the concert hall hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it posts a real salaried payroll vacancy with a wage and start in writing. I used to check its ticket cash, but familiarity with the manager does not create a funded desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Elise that the concert package can wait while we put cash beside the rent and groceries. I wouldn't ask our grown children to make up my wage.

I'd ask for **real funded vacancies** at the hall.
think: I expect my **junior post** to end quickly when AGI takes routine venue accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hall managers five years gives us time to compare real refund records and decide whether a person is still worth paying to sign them. Full AGI reaches the tax desk in 2031, while robots at the ticket gate come about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be sixty-three and still need a wage, even with ten months saved today. A ticket booth is physical, but the payroll and cash thinking there changes in 2031; I would not retrain for a job title with no paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a written retirement-income estimate and ask West Arch each season whether signed refund reviews still bring in fees. In the first year after 2031, if my post ends and wages are still needed, I'd apply for a posted salaried concert-hall payroll role with written bill-covering pay and start date, keeping any paid West Arch work only while offered until the new job starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about whether the firm can still pay for the checks I know. Five years is useful for numbers, but a paper estimate won't hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a payroll course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid hall role requires it and the hall funds the fee and paid study time. I have a bachelor's degree in accounting already; I won't spend our reserve on a course for a vacancy that is only rumoured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall posts no payroll role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep any paid West Arch returns still offered and look at the other firms with real openings. I would not tell my partner Elise that the venue manager's friendly nod is a start date.

I'd separate **2031 payroll thinking** from 2034 gate robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners a decade gives us time to check real retirement income and the fees clients still pay for an accountable return. Full AGI reaches the accounts desk in 2036; physical gate robots come about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may have left paid work, but I cannot promise that before we see written income and regular bills. Ten months saved today is strong, yet it is not proof of an income for every later year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the written retirement-income estimate and compare it with our household bills each autumn while taking paid West Arch returns. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials I'd stay within that budget; if wages are still needed and the firm ends my post, I'd apply for posted paid hall payroll only with written bill-covering pay and a start date, keeping any paid West Arch work only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant desk risk, though we have time and nearby firms. I won't count retirement as funded until written income and household bills are on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Elise's library hours fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra home-repair saving and pay food and rent from current wages first. The reserve is there for a gap, not a target to keep filling when one wage falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work at the gate instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My tax desk changes in 2036, and the physical gate could change when robots arrive around 2039. I would choose a real posted payroll vacancy over a story about safe gate work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because venue accounts could lose the junior desk before I know if retirement income covers us. A real posted paid job with written wages and a start would help, as would paid returns while West Arch still offers them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells a promoter why the night's cash doesn't match the ticket count. The missing refund will still have a customer at the window after the report is printed.

headlineQuote: The missing refund will still have a customer at the window after the report is printed.
portrait: Erik, **fifty-eight**, is a junior venue accountant who enjoys reconciling refunds and dislikes crumpled till rolls.
He has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning tax work and uses tested AI notes occasionally.
Higher pay, **ten months saved** and plenty of local firms provide a strong but finite cushion.
He learns **new matching controls** only on paid supervised time after error checks.
Retirement depends on **verified income**; AGI could end his junior desk before physical gate robots.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028** ending his paid desk before retirement income is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid current work** and a posted salaried opening with written bill-covering wage and start.
